physical_harm: Multiple injuries leading to death due to shock and haemorrhage from ante mortem incised wounds
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the incriminating circumstances were not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the last seen circumstance was inconclusive, thereby justifying the High Court's acquittal.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, particularly PW-2, as doubtful and unreliable, suggesting that the witness was set up to create link evidence.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was last seen alive in his own house in the company of the accused at about 7.00 p.m. on 10.12.1998, the dead body was found by PW-6 on 12.12.1998, the accused made an extra-judicial confession before PW-3, and disclosed the location of the knife used in the crime, which was recovered. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court was justified in acquitting the accused because the incriminating circumstances were not proved beyond reasonable doubt, the last seen circumstance was inconclusive, the recovery of the knife was doubtful, and the extra-judicial confession lacked credibility.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that to convict an accused on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must prove each incriminating circumstance beyond reasonable doubt, forming a chain so complete that it excludes all other hypotheses consistent with the accused's innocence.
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Sahai (1982) 1 SCC 352; State of M.P. v. Paltan Mallah (2005) 3 SCC 169; Basheera Begam v. Mohd. Ibrahim (2020) 11 SCC 174; Shivaji Chintappa Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021) 5 SCC 626
